title: Origins of Strata-East, Pharoah Sanders, Clifford Jordan and Gil Scott-Heron
summary: Tolliver corrects the claim that Strata-East grew from the Civil Rights movement: Blue Note never gave him or Woody Shaw a date, so he and Stanley Cowell launched their own label in 1970. Clifford Jordan hands over his Pharoah Sanders recording and Gil Scott-Heron brings a finished record.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Record labels, producers and the business of making albums

blocks.x: Let’s talk about Strata-East. I’m going to read another quote about the label. This was a description: “Strata-East operated on a minimal finance and maximal passion, a pivotal platform for the independent jazz movement that emerged from the Civil Rights in the 1970s.” And before that they had mentioned Pharaoh Sanders as being on the label with one album I guess, and they called him one of the leaders of the movement. So my question is did you and Stanley Cowell feel that your label was part of some movement?

Well there are three things in what you just read which need to be clarified. Let’s put it that way. The label that it was to become wasn’t created because, again, of the political or social environment going on. So you know what you said about, can you read that again so I can —
Yeah, just read what you read.
Okay. “Operated on a minimal finances, maximal passion, a pivotal platform for the independent jazz movement that emerged from Civil Rights in the 1970s.

Okay. Okay. It didn’t emerge from the Civil Rights Movement because my idea to do an independent endeavor like this stemmed from let’s say two events. First of all, when I was coming up and you really got into this, you either got your own leader date at Blue Note or one of the other independents that was going on at the time. That didn’t happen to me nor did it happen for Woody Shaw, because both of us were coming up at the same time. It should have, you know, because of who we recorded with on Blue Note. Both of us recorded with Jackie McLean and Horace Silver, and both worked in the Horace Silver band and Max Roach as well. But Alfred Lion sold Blue Note records in 1966, right? Or ’65. And he didn’t get around to giving us a record date. Things would be

completely different in terms of the historical thing of my career had that happened. So by 1968, ’69, I was already, I already had this what was going to become Strata-East records. I was going to do it, it was just a matter of time. And because my dear Stanley Cowell and I were so close you know, every day, and working with Max Roach and watching what he did it was inevitable at that particular time, in 1970, that we were going to go in the studio and make a recording which would be the first record to launch the label and it had nothing to do with anything else but us finally putting out a product under our own name and see where it goes you know? In fact I shopped it first to the independents but it was a big band record so they weren’t biting on it and I didn’t care because I was going to do it anyway. So it had absolutely nothing to do with that first part of what you just read, and I appreciate that they could read into that that it did because it happened right when the country was steaming. And LBJ, as he was told by his famous Senate colleague, you know if you do this you’ll lose the South. And that’s exactly what happened, politically. But I wasn’t, that didn’t factor in you know, or the unrest and of course the riots that happened, you know, with Martin Luther King’s death and everything. Everything was already incubated to do what we were going to do with Strata-East before any of that happened. Now I don’t know if, Pharoah Sanders was a part of the free jazz movement, but he was going to be who he became anyway. Let’s put it this way, I think they were all obviously they’ve said this, without John Coltrane that would not have happened. And so the reason why Pharaoh Sanders’ recording landed with Strata-East was because of the great Clifford Jordan. I mean actually the — when Clifford Jordan saw what we did with the first recording he said to me, he said, “You know I’ve already done that.” And he had. He had already recorded Pharaoh Sanders and four others, which he called the Dolphy Series. And he said, “Hey, here you go, run with it.” So Clifford Jordan was as important as anything that ever we came with in Strata-East because it helped to further jumpstart this venture. And of course Pharoah Sanders’ record was one of them and so it became, you know, one of the signature issues, you know, of the label. But — and I’ll just go on with this since we’re on this Strata-East topic, now after about two years in all the musicians’ ears started to prop up, you know, what’s going on with this Strata-East thing you know. And you know one day, you know, a guy walked into the office named Gil Scott Heron and he said, “I want to do that too.” He had, like everybody else, was required to already have done their product. We created a conduit by which it would get to the marketplace. And of course the rest is history with that one because it just so happened that he had one track on there that took off.
